title: Five steps, one slow clock
scenario: A retail team runs a weekly price check on the Claude Agent SDK. A lead agent starts subagents to read three competitor stores, then builds a table and writes a summary. The run takes too long, and a quick question once cost far too much. You read the task list and the logs (exhibit). The team, the tasks and every number are made up for this case.
exhibit:
TASKS (made up for this case)
  T1  read store A price page          40 s   needs: nothing
  T2  read store B price page          55 s   needs: nothing
  T3  read store C price page          35 s   needs: nothing
  T4  build comparison table           30 s   needs: T1, T2, T3 results
  T5  write summary                    20 s   needs: T4 result

CURRENT RUN
  all five tasks run one after another: 40 + 55 + 35 + 30 + 20 = 180 s

LOG (made up)
  10-03  Store B's page hung for 20 minutes. T4 and T5 never started.
  10-04  Finance: "No more than 5 subagents should run at once."

questions.prompt: Which steps can run in parallel without losing any information?

options.text: T3 and T4, because T4 can start when store C is ready.
options.explanation: T4 needs the results of T1, T2 and T3. Starting it early would build the table from missing data.

options.text: T4 and T5, because the summary can be written while the table is built.
options.explanation: T5 needs the table from T4. Without it, the summary has nothing to describe.

options.text: T1, T2 and T3, because none of them needs another task's result.
options.explanation: Right. These are independent subtasks, the case where parallel work helps. T4 and T5 depend on earlier results.

options.text: All five, with T4 and T5 retrying until the reads finish.
options.explanation: Retries burn calls while waiting. T4 and T5 still depend on earlier results.

questions.prompt: T1, T2 and T3 run in parallel, then T4 and T5 run in order. About how long does the run take?

options.explanation: Right. The parallel part takes as long as the slowest task, 55 s. Then T4 (30 s) and T5 (20 s) follow: 55 + 30 + 20 = 105.
That is the sum of all five tasks. It is the current sequential time, not the parallel time.
That counts only the slowest store read. T4 and T5 still have to run after it.
That is 40 + 55 + 35, the sum of the three reads. Parallel reads take the time of the slowest one instead.

questions.prompt: On 10-03 the whole run waited on one slow read. Why, and what fits the Anthropic engineering post?

options.text: The lead waits for each set of workers; give each a stop rule.
options.explanation: Right. The Anthropic engineering post says synchronous execution creates bottlenecks: the system can be blocked by one subagent. A stop rule keeps one worker from blocking the rest.

options.text: The lead was out of context, so it needs a longer window to continue.
options.explanation: The log shows a hung page, not a full context. A longer window would not end the wait.

options.text: Parallel agents cannot be stopped, so remove store B from the plan for good.
options.explanation: Dropping a store loses data forever. Anthropic's note is about waiting, which a stop rule can bound.

options.text: The reads ran in parallel, so the slowest one cannot affect the total time.
options.explanation: The opposite is true. Parallel work takes the time of the slowest worker, so a hung worker holds up the run.

questions.prompt: Finance wants at most 5 subagents running at once in the Claude Agent SDK. Which setting does that?

options.text: Set `max_turns` to 5, so each run stops after five round trips.
options.explanation: `max_turns` caps tool-use round trips for the run. It does not limit how many subagents run at once.
Right. At the limit, a new spawn fails with `Concurrent subagent limit reached` until the running count drops.

options.text: Set `max_budget_usd` to 5, so each run stops at five dollars.
options.explanation: That caps spend in dollars. A run could still start many subagents before it reaches the cap.
That limits how deeply subagents can nest, not how many run at the same time.
